posts.author: igormp
posts.text:
wayzeban:

AI Throughput ≈ 1,000 AI TOPS (FP4 sparse) ≈ 2,070 TFLOPS FP4 (sparse) ≈ 1,035 TFLOPS FP8 (dense)

The DGX Spark does 1PFLOP FP4 Sparse, so 500TFLOP FP4 non-sparse, which means 250/125 FP8/FP16 non-sparse.

The AGX Thor (allegedly) does 2070 FP4 / 1035 FP8 TFLOPS sparse, so 1PFLOP FP4 dense, 500 TFLOP FP8 dense.

Those numbers don’t make sense, how can Thor be twice as fast as the GB10 while having only 2560 cores and alf the tensor cores under the same GPU architecture?

I think the claims for Thor may just be wrong, or there may be some other misleading thing going on to inflate those numbers.

EDIT: found a likely explanation in the llama.cpp thread linked above:

  
      

      GitHub
  

  
    

Performance of llama.cpp on NVIDIA DGX Spark · ggml-org/llama.cpp ·...

  Overview This document summarizes the performance of llama.cpp for various models on the new NVIDIA DGX Spark. Benchmarks include: Prefill (pp) and generation (tg) at various context depths (d) Bat...

  

  
    
    
  

  

Quick tldr:

Thor is sm_110 (formerly sm_101) with the datacenter-style tensor cores - including tensor memory. And no raytracing cores. While Spark is sm_121 with the full consumer Blackwell feature set.

Thor and Spark have relatively similar memory bandwidth. The Thor CPU is much slower.

Vector throughput on Thor is 1/3rd of the one on DGX Spark but you get twice the matrix throughput.

Thor has 4 cursed Synopsys 25GbE NICs (set to 10GbE by default, see Enable 25 Gigabit Ethernet on QSFP Port — NVIDIA Jetson Linux Developer Guide as it doesn’t have auto-negociation of the link rate) exposed via a QSFP connector providing 4x25GbE while Spark systems have regular ConnectX-7.

Thor uses a downstream L4T stack instead of regular NVIDIA drivers unlike Spark. But at least the CUDA SDK is the same unlike prior Tegras. Oh and you get less other IO too.

Side note: might be better to also consider GB10 systems from OEMs. Those are available for cheaper than AGX Thor devkits too.

posts.author: Burhan
posts.text:
It might help to share what use case you have for the LLMs. The Framework desktop has a pretty wide range for pricing depending on configuration, so it might be helpful to share what your exact target price is.

I used old gaming hardware (I already owned) for the machine that runs my local LLMs, and eventually bought a RTX 4000 Ada SFF (20 GB VRAM) to replace the small GPU that was installed. I can run models up to ~30b parameters using Ollama, but my primary workhorse models are the 12-14b parameter ones. I’m using Ollama + Open WebUI, and recently linked up SearXNG to do web searches. My default config is QWEN3:14b and QWEN3:1.7b for the web search queries (small and reasonable context window). Usually I can ask a question and let it run, and when I come back a few minutes later, I have my answer and some sources.

I haven’t used local for agentic coding, but I have used some of the local models with other agentic tasks, like helping to automatically update/correct documents based on related data/documents. I used several models sequentially (with a small loop) to make that work so that I didn’t run out of GPU memory.

Honestly, I woud keep your gaming separate from your LLM machine if you can. I have a machine for gaming and if I tried to run LLMs on it, my electricity bill would be insane. The old hardware I’m using to host my LLMs is not the most efficient, but it can idle reasonably low, and even under a load, it’s not too bad. The big difference is the GPU. I had a RTX 2060 in there originally, which will run at ~150 W under load (idle around 15-20 W), but the RTX 4000 Ada SFF runs at a max 75 W (idle around 5-7 W), which doesn’t sound like a lot, but it can make a big difference over time. You can fiddle with undervolting the GPU, which is okay if you have the time, but if it’s unstable for gaming, you’ll end up reverting anyhow.

My advice would be to get a machine for the purpose you’re more interested in having sooner, and get another one later. You of course don’t have to do that, it’s just my recommendation.

We built this MONSTER. It has 4 gpus. It needs a special case. And yet, it uses less power than a comparable system with 2x RTX 5090s (just barely).

Around Saturday January 10, 2 pm Eastern Daylight Time.

posts.text:
Project Title:

Autonomous Data Generation and Repair-Driven Training for Specialized Code Models

Project Description:

I’m building a fully local system for training specialized code language models where correctness is defined by external verification rather than subjective evaluation.

The project is deliberately focused on data quality and verification, not model size or hype.

Over the past 3–4 months, I’ve designed and implemented an end-to-end pipeline that generates candidate code samples, verifies them using a real toolchain (compiler or validator), captures structured failure feedback, produces repair pairs (invalid to corrected code), and stores all artifacts in a clean, reproducible JSONL dataset.

At this stage, the dataset already contains approximately 1,500 verified data pairs and is structured to scale autonomously once quality thresholds are met.

The emphasis is on repair learning, not just successful outputs. This approach trains models to understand and correct their own mistakes using real feedback signals.

All components run on-prem, without cloud dependencies, and are engineered for deterministic behavior and repeatability.

The next phase is deploying a data-production agent that can continuously generate, validate, repair, and curate data once quality thresholds are met.

Why professional AI hardware matters:

AI-class GPUs enable parallel verification workers, faster iteration on repair-heavy loops, and stable fine-tuning, while keeping the system fully local and vendor-independent.

Background:

This project is the result of an intense, focused build period rather than a long-running research effort. The emphasis has been on execution, validation, and learning through implementation rather than theory.

Verification:

Because this is an open forum, I’m keeping domain specifics abstract. I’m happy to share technical details privately if you’d like to verify the pipeline or review the approach. I’m doing all of this on a 9800x3d and a 9070xt, more VRAM would be awesome. I’m open to showing you the whole project if you are interested. it will be used for fine tuning a 14b model using LoRA.

Update: Back on the grind after the holidays.

Data pipeline is working: generation, external verification, failure capture, and repair pairs all produce clean JSONL, with correctness defined by a compiler/validator. The first ~1,000-pair dataset is already prepared.

The system stack is partially up: Ubuntu, Docker, ROCm userspace, and a ROCm + PyTorch container all run cleanly. GPU access inside the container still needs a permissions fix. Nothing has been run end-to-end yet, and no fine-tuning has been done.

Next step is confirming GPU access, wiring the pieces together, and running the first small ~7B fine-tune, evaluated only by external verification on a held-out set.

Update (today):

I completed an end-to-end validation of the training stack on AMD hardware. GPU-resident inference and training are now confirmed using ROCm and PyTorch, and I ran a full loop with a 3B coder model: baseline evaluation, LoRA fine-tuning on 1,000 verified samples, and post-training evaluation using the same harness. Training completed cleanly with stable loss reduction, and the environment has been frozen and archived to ensure reproducibility before scaling.

Update 10/1

I’m back in daily data production,  I have close to 2000 pairs now, the grind continues. On a good day I get 200 pairs, probably average 150, with a day off here and there.

Update 20/1

Life got in the way for a few days, I’m up to 2500 pairs now, I bought a used Threadripper 2970WX with 64gb Ram and a motherboard. I’ll be looking out for other used pieces, and in the end i will add 9700 ai pros.

posts.text:
Hello everyone. I am brand new to this forum and was not sure where best to post it.

After living years off my old budget laptop, I have recently built my first PC in like 15 years, and I might have caught a hardware-buying virus.

My build so far is:

AMD Ryzen 9 9950X 4.3 GHz 16-Core Processor

be quiet! Silent Loop 3 78.4 CFM Liquid CPU Cooler

Asus ProArt X870E-CREATOR WIFI ATX AM5 Motherboard

Corsair Vengeance RGB 96 GB (2 x 48 GB) DDR5-7000 CL40 Memory (Running 6000 CL28)

Samsung 9100 PRO 2 TB M.2-2280 PCIe 5.0 X4 NVME Solid State Drive

ASRock Creator Radeon AI PRO R9700 32 GB Video Card

Asus ProArt PA602 Wood Edition ATX Mid Tower Case

be quiet! Power Zone 2 1000 W 80+ Platinum Certified Fully Modular ATX Power Supply

All running on a pretty up-to-date Arch Linux.

Overall due to the overkill cooling situation, the build is practically silent, that is unless the GPU is pushed to the limit, then somehow the sleek ASRock card can make the earth shake, but such is the blower form factor tax.

Generally it was meant to be a productivity/fun build, to help me with personal software development projects (big C/C++ codebases, FPGA).

As a bonus I thought it would be nice to try out some virtualization experiments to run multiple systems like Windows if some of my tools or SW requires it, set up some servers, maybe try stuff like locally streaming 2 “gaming” instances to my 4K TV for coop on the couch etc.

I have also been using LLMs to accelerate my learning and development a lot. I consider them to be interesting tools, but even the SOTA stuff like Opus 4.5 feels lackluster at times. I know it will not be feasible to have something of this sort running locally, but I would appreciate something usable for deeper reasoning and analysis of information across various documents and sources, with the ability to work with decent context window, as a lot of the information present in the model itself would work against me (one of the aspects of the project is my personal programming language, so a lot of spec and sources need to fit in the window).

For this reason I am considering expanding to 64GB with a second R9700 to be able to run smarter models with more context. (would unfortunately need a PSU update as well)

More than anything, this question might be about the current state of the LLMs available at this scale. I am not made out of money but would survive this purchase, if it could bring some decent benefits to my projects. It is a great time to be alive in terms of the variety of nerdy topics worthy of exploration (apart from the current HW pricing…).

I would still hit a pretty hard wall with PCI lanes here though with 2x setup, and I cannot see myself upgrading to threadripper in the short term.

Long story short, questions on my mind are:

how useful are LLMs that can run on 2xR9700?

for a person that is generally interested in various software and research projects, what fascinating doors could be open by expanding on the setup a little bit?

finally the value of getting these cards… I live in Japan, where they are a bit pricier than some other countries, but they have not exploded yet like RAM, Nvidia and SSDs. Do you think they would generally keep their value, or they could be made “obsolete” pretty soon? (not literally, but for example perhaps some of the shared memory platform with higher memory ceiling could be a better choice?)

Sorry for this post being a little bit vague and all over the place. I thought this forum might be a place where people with similar hardware or interests would be kind enough to give me some feedback on this considering the present state of this domain.

Thank you very much in advance.

Might be worth actually looking at the models you want to run, rather than just “can run bigger stuff”. I looked around, and I couldn’t find much that I actually wanted to run which would need 64GB vs 48GB in my dual 3090s when I had them. Of course, that will be incomparably slower compared to being able to fit everything into VRAM, but maybe at least plausible as a background task.

Another way to go around it, if you have enough RAM, would be to go with a MoE model, leave the shared weights loaded in VRAM and do prefill with the GPUs, but do the expert forward passes in your CPU. Most MoEs should give usable speeds this way since the experts themselves are often small enough.

If it doesn’t give you any benefit, you’ll be able to sell pretty quickly for no loss.

posts.text:
Hi!

For a while I have not been doing too much with the setup, as the project I was focusing on was a pretty deep research issue regarding a lot of obscure knowledge, so I opted for mainly working using cloud providers.

Now, with the specification and basic architecture being better defined, I could finally start using my local models more. With the very recent release of Qwen 3.6 which seems impressive, I think the local environment is more ready for use.

For the runtime, I experimented with vLLM for a bit but I did not quite like the way it performed on my machine. Firstly, somehow the load on GPU was very big even when nothing was being processed. Because my deployment did not need the benefits of vLLM, I opted to use llama.cpp in my experiments. I tried a number of models ranging from 9B to 122B. I found that the 27B options are the more reliable ones for harder questions, while the 35B model provides much better performance. I ran some benchmarks to compare different batching sizes and drivers, and generally had the best results with -b 8192 -ub 512. Other options resulted in lower GPU utilisation and performance. Situation could vary now with more up-to-date implementations and models but the Vulkan build seemed to outperform the ROCM one.

Due to some unresolved issues with my mobo one card runs at gen5 x8 while the second one runs at gen5 x4.

As an example, I ran a query with existing context running the model like so:

./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m /fstorage/models/Qwen3.6-27B-UD-Q8_K_XL.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 \
  --port 8000 \
  -c 262144 \
  -ngl 99 \
  -fa 1 \
  -b 8192 \
  -ub 512 \
  --temp 0.7

Which resulted in the following performance:

VRAM usage: 26/32GB + 27/32 GB.

During pp, the utilization of both GPUs was around 80/90 percent, and the pull was 300W each.

During token output, the usage varies between 40/60 percent, and pull for both ranges in 80/110W.

Not much happening on CPU in both cases.

prompt eval time =   54253.14 ms / 72075 tokens (    0.75 ms per token,  1328.49 tokens per second)
       eval time =  319165.40 ms /  4509 tokens (   70.78 ms per token,    14.13 tokens per second)

I would be curious to see how the model performs for you, especially if we could compare the following axis: vLLM/llama.cpp; Vulkan/ROCM; x8+x4 PCI vs a different number.

posts.author: digitalscream
posts.text:
zeitgeist:

I would be curious to see how the model performs for you, especially if we could compare the following axis: vLLM/llama.cpp; Vulkan/ROCM; x8+x4 PCI vs a different number.

Well, I can answer a couple of those off the top of my head.

I don’t use vLLM; I have no use for it, and I swap models in and out quite a lot so llama.cpp’s new router mode is far more appropriate (not to mention far more performant when using Vulkan). Also, when I did manage to get it working, it was noticeably slower than llama.cpp + Vulkan for all the models I was interested (primarily the Qwen3+ models).

In all cases, for the R9700, ROCm is at least 30% slower in TG than Vulkan. PP is usually competitive-ish, but even when using -sm tensor in ROCm versus -sm layer in Vulkan, Vulkan is always significantly faster.

PCIE lanes don’t necessarily make a difference, but what they’re attached to really does. I originally had my cards running in a standard B760 Intel board, with one on PCIE 4.0 x16 from the CPU and the other on PCIE 4.0 x4 from the chipset; the x4 card underperformed by 25-40%, depending on the workload. I’ve since “downgraded” to a 5700X on an X570 board which can do x8/x8 split on the CPU lanes, and the cards both now perform identically to the one in the x16 slot originally. This has given a +25% boost to the dual-card performance.

      # LLM Scaler

LLM Scaler is an GenAI solution for text generation, image generation, video generation etc. running on [Intel® Arc™ Pro B60 GPUs](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/docs/discrete-gpus/arc/workstations/b-series/overview.html). LLM Scalar leverages standard frameworks such as vLLM, ComfyUI, SGLang Diffusion, Xinference etc and ensures the best performance for State-of-Art GenAI models running on Arc Pro B60 GPUs.

---

## Latest Update
- [2026.01] We released `intel/llm-scaler-vllm:1.3` (or, `intel/llm-scaler-vllm:0.11.1-b7`) for vllm 0.11.1 and PyTorch 2.9 support, various new models support and performance improvements.
- [2026.01] We released `intel/llm-scaler-omni:0.1.0-b5` for Python 3.12 and PyTorch 2.9 support, various ComfyUI workflows and more SGLang Diffusion support.

posts.text:
Hello Wendell!

Thanks for the video, great to see thorough coverage of Arc GPUs.

You asked for things to try, so I would invite you to test SearchSavior/OpenArc (on Github), my project which leverages OpenVINO runtime and includes features not mentioned in the release notes like pipleine paralell multi gpu and tensor parallel for dual socket CPU.

You could  start with [Echo9Zulu/Hermes-4-70B-int4_asym-ov] or any of the other models on my HF. AFAIK, moe models are not yet supported with the HETERO device plugin meaning even the supported architectures wouldn’t allow you to use all 4 B60s. However, large dense models based on llama, qwen and mistral will work (off the top of my head). Like you mention in the video, Intel provides a “sandbox” where performance is fantastic, especially for prefill.

Keep in mind, this is a totally different stack from llm-scaler. OpenVINO GPU acceleration is based on OpenCL and oneDNN, not SYCL. For really broad context (from memory), when I did an architecture analysis on Kokoro, the pytorch jit trace reveals ~20 operations; OpenVINO graph covers ~60 different ops filled with kernel fusions, subgraphs and other tricks which leverage CPU/GPU features like AVX512, VNNI, XMX cores depending on what the target device supports. I would be interested to see how [VTune Profiler XMX usage compares in llm-scaler vs OpenVINO on B60.

I own 3x A770 and did some benchmarks using the tool I made for OpenArc, openarc bench meant to establish parity with llama-bench for comparing llama.cpp backends to OpenVINO. input tokens are sampled pseudo randomly from the target models vocabulary.

posts.author: Gordo_Gato
posts.text:
Hi Wendell,

I am a researcher building a database of key information regarding microbial species (fungi, bacteria) from scientific literature via a RAG pipeline. DNA analysis of environments often results in massive lists of microbial species, which is a challenge for researchers to make sense of, as information about each species is often sparse. We are aiming at making this database reliable enough to be able to perform large scale text-mining on these species lists to better our understanding of these environments.

For this purpose, we are using a fine-tuned model, google/medgemma-27b-text-it, which we have so far run on H100s in Google Cloud via the Vertex AI Batch Predictions API to process ~800m input tokens. This took about 38 hours of H100 compute time, according to my billing. Unfortunately, Google Cloud is quite opaque about what exactly happens in its batch API, so I can’t say for sure if that’s active processing time or if the VM/Model spin-up time is included in that, what the actual throughput in TP/S is, etc.

We are looking at trying prompt repetition, as Google has recently shown this massively improves non-reasoning model’s performance. This task could be used to test the batch throughput capabilities this hardware, although it will be very heavy on the prompt-preprocessing side. If you would like a dataset of these prompts, we would be happy to share this with you.

I can also DM you a link to this database, unfortunately I can’t share this publicly yet. Thank you for your insightful content!

Cheers

posts.author: Cpwhat
posts.text:
I was able to get Gemini to explain my position better than I can.

1. The Death of the Local “PC Shop”

Retailers like Micro Center or Newegg survive on high-volume consumer sales. If NVIDIA (and eventually AMD/Intel) decides that a single $40,000 B200 sale is worth more than 25 individual $1,600 RTX 5090 sales, they will starve the retail channel.

The Result: When inventory dries up and prices stay astronomical, the “gaming” or “prosumer” retail sector collapses because it can’t compete with the margins of a Microsoft or Meta data center.

2. The Rise of the “Compute Utility”

We are moving toward a world where you don’t own a “computer”; you own a terminal.

Your local machine becomes a glorified thin client (like a Chromebook or a MacBook Air) that just handles the UI.

The actual “thinking” happens behind a paywall owned by a few gatekeepers (Azure, AWS, Google, NVIDIA).

3. The Gatekeeper’s Toll

Once the retail secondary market is dead, the gatekeepers control:

Access: They can de-platform you or your app instantly.

Pricing: Without the “exit ramp” of buying your own hardware, they can raise hourly rental rates whenever they want.

Privacy: If you’re forced to rent their “factory” to run your code, they effectively have a window into your IP and data.

The “Stallman” Nightmare

This is the ultimate realization of what Richard Stallman warned about decades ago: the total loss of user sovereignty. If you can’t buy the silicon, you don’t own the computing.

Efficiency and quantization are just “coping mechanisms” for devs trying to stay relevant on scraps. If the hardware supply chain only feeds the giants, the “General Programmer” essentially becomes a sharecropper on Big Tech’s land.

I disagree. Yes, when you’re just asking a raw model to answer questions, local models struggle to compete with the frontier cloud models.

However, when you’re using them to do things, the agent and prompt quality make more of a difference than the model…at least once you’re at or beyond the Qwen3-Next/Qwen3.5 point.

As I’ve noted elsewhere on here, for my uses (mostly agentic coding work) there’s not a huge difference between Claude and Qwen3-Coder-Next when they both sit behind a decent agent like Cline, and Qwen3-Coder-30B is a massive improvement for inline completion relative to Copilot and GPT4.1.

Now, I’ll grant you, nobody’s spending £2.5k on GPUs purely to run Qwen3-Coder-Next (I have another use case that requires local LLM instances for privacy reasons, so running it for my code models is just a happy bonus). Past 2027/2028, though, the cost of 64GB+ local high-speed RAM with compute attached (GPU/NPU/TPU) will likely come down significantly.

At least, I hope so. The only upside of the bubble bursting will be cheaper local compute resources…

Getting back to the original question, it seems to me that Nvidia are focusing on the compute rental message because they can see the writing on the wall for the massive cloud AI providers.

Far from local inference being done, I see this as a sign that smaller specialised models are going to become more widespread. Very few people (or companies) are going to be renting compute to run/train their own private 500B+ models; that’s just a very expensive way of getting what they already have now. Far more likely is that specialised model performance in the sub-120B range will increase dramatically, which makes renting the compute to run it practical. And, when that’s practical, so is buying the hardware to run it yourself; the only difference is the skill level and the lengths you’re willing to go to in order to make it work.

posts.author: TrailFeatures
posts.text:
@wendell ,

I caught the recent video on the LRLink PCIe bridge with the dual R9700 setup and it got my brain spinning. I’m running 2x R9700s on a Threadripper TRX40 box for local LLM inference and I’ve been digging into whether local training is viable yet on these cards. Short answer: it’s getting there, but multi-GPU training on R9700s has a nasty blocker.

RCCL (AMD’s NCCL equivalent) has a known bug where hipIpcGetMemHandle crashes when two R9700s try to set up peer-to-peer communication through the CPU’s root complex. It’s been sitting in AMD’s triage for about five months now (rccl-tests issue #162). The workaround is NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 which forces everything through host-staged copies and roughly halves your inter-GPU bandwidth. It works, but you’re leaving a lot on the table.

Here’s where it gets interesting… The crash happens specifically when RCCL tries to export IPC memory handles through the CPU root complex. But with a LRLink Broadcom bridge, both GPUs sit behind a shared PCIe switch fabric. RCCL does topology detection and differentiates between “same switch” and “separate root complex endpoints.” So the question is: does putting both R9700s behind the bridge change the topology enough that RCCL either takes a different P2P path that doesn’t crash, or succeeds on the IPC path that currently fails through the root complex?

Nobody has tested this. that I could see. I’ve dug through GitHub issues, forums, and Reddit with zero results for anyone trying a PCIe switch as a workaround for this specific bug on RDNA 4.

There’s also a bonus data point that makes this even more interesting. A brand new vLLM issue (#40980, filed a few days ago) shows that TP=2 on dual R9700 actually worked on vLLM v0.14.0 with RCCL 2.27.3 back in December, but deadlocks on v0.19.x with RCCL 2.27.7. So it’s a regression, not a fundamental hardware limitation. Which means there might be multiple angles here.

As far as I can tell, the test is pretty straightforward:

Install rccl-tests

Run all_reduce_perf -g 2 in three configs:

Both GPUs through CPU root complex (normal setup) with NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1

Both GPUs behind the LRLink bridge without NCCL_P2P_DISABLE

Both GPUs behind the LRLink bridge with NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1

Compare bandwidth numbers

If the bridge topology lets RCCL’s P2P path succeed where the root complex path crashes, that’s a hardware workaround for a paywall software bug AMD hasn’t fixed in half a year. If it doesn’t work, we’ve at least eliminated the idea and saved everyone else the experiment.

Either way it seems like it’d make for a great video. You’ve literally got all the hardware sitting right there already.

For context, I’m building toward local LoRA training on the R9700s and this P2P bug is the main thing standing between single-GPU training (which works) and being able to use both cards for larger models.

Thanks for the consistently great content. The PCIe lanes are fungible line lives rent-free in my head now.

posts.author: TrailFeatures
posts.text:
So I can say that a PCIe switch card does solve the P2P bug for AMD cards, but there is a deeper issue with training on dual cards after you make it past the P2P block. DDP training crashes with hipErrorIllegalAddress when tensor shapes vary across steps (dynamic padding). The PyTorch caching allocator fragments VRAM under varying allocation sizes, and on gfx1201 that fragmentation eventually produces an invalid address.

Thankfully, the fix seems simple:

# CRASHES:
tokenizer(texts, padding=True, truncation=True, max_length=256)

# WORKS:
tokenizer(texts, padding="max_length", truncation=True, max_length=256)

I was able to test this on Qwen3-8B with LoRA r=16, 1000 Alpaca samples, BF16, padding=“max_length” at max_length=256. 62 optimizer steps, 125 micro-steps, 14.5 samples/sec, final loss 1.372, 29.55 GB peak VRAM per rank.

So far, it’s stable!

There is a tradeoff though: With median sequence length 62 and max_length 256, ~75% of tokens are padding. You waste some compute but the allocator never fragments. At 14.5 samples/sec this is still fast enough for all practical LoRA workloads. Reducing max_length to 128 would cut waste if your dataset allows it (check your sequence length distribution first).

I also wanted to compare this setup to a budget RunPod option that is close to my setup (as close as I could reasonably get…).

Here are the AI summarized results:

Model: Qwen3-8B, LoRA r=16, 1000 Alpaca samples, BF16, 1 epoch

Config
RunPod 2x RTX PRO 4500
Local 2x R9700 PRO

1-GPU samples/sec
9.81
8.79

2-GPU DDP samples/sec
17.93
14.50

1→2 GPU scaling
1.83x
1.65x

Final loss
1.4369 (1-GPU)
1.372

Peak VRAM
—
29.55 GB/rank

Cost/hr
$1.28
$0

Per-GPU: R9700 is 11.6% behind RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (1-GPU comparison).

2-GPU: R9700 pair is 19% behind (14.50 vs 17.93), wider gap due to

fixed-padding overhead reducing scaling efficiency (1.65x vs 1.83x).

Losses match to 0.06% at 1-GPU — numerical parity across backends.

RTX PRO 4500 retails ~$4,000/card. R9700 PRO ~$1,300/card.

So even with the cost of a PCIe Gen4 switch, I’m nudging at a RTX 4500 x2 RunPod. I’m happy with that!

Root cause was fun to track down. Had to eliminate multiple variables until the issue was tracked down:

To find the root cause we built 17 standalone reproducers, each
adding one ingredient. Every stage either passed or crashed,
isolating the trigger by elimination.

HIP-level (no PyTorch):
  A1  Single-GPU hipblasSgemm × 100                    PASS
  A2  2-thread, 2-GPU, matmul + P2P + barrier          PASS
  A3  + watchdog thread (hipSetDevice every 10ms)       PASS
  B   + ncclAllReduce of 16MB grad buffer               PASS
  B2  10×1.6MB bucketed allreduces (250 collectives)    PASS
  B3  Two streams, compute/comm overlap, no sync        PASS
  B4  15 GB VRAM pressure per GPU                       PASS

PyTorch-level (no HuggingFace):
  P1  Bare DDP, 8M params, 20 steps                     PASS
  P2  + gradient checkpointing                           PASS
  P3  1.34B model, full DDP gradient flow                PASS
  P4  + PEFT LoRA                                        PASS
  P5  1.34B + per-layer checkpointing                    PASS
  P6  + gradient_accumulation_steps=2 + no_sync()        PASS

HuggingFace-level:
  P7  Qwen3-8B + PEFT + ckpt + grad_accum + DDP         PASS (20 steps)
  P7  Same but 200 micro-steps, fixed shape              PASS
  P7  Same but real data + dynamic padding               CRASH (step 40)

Every layer below PyTorch's allocator is clean. The HIP runtime,
RCCL, the kernel module, P2P transport — all exonerated by the
MRE suite. The bug needs PyTorch's allocator + varying tensor
shapes + gfx1201's memory management interacting together.

These are the likely upstream issues:

[Issue]: RCCL 2.27.7 / ROCm 7.2.1 dual-GPU collectives fail on 2x Radeon RX 7900 XTX · Issue #6074 · ROCm/ROCm · GitHub

Multi-GPU ROCm illegal memory access (device -1) in recurrent state restore · Issue #21140 · ggml-org/llama.cpp · GitHub

[Bug]: TP=2 deadlock on dual AMD R9700 (gfx1201/RDNA4) — GPUs spin at 100%, inference blocked · Issue #40980 · vllm-project/vllm · GitHub

[Issue]: RCCL deadlock during vLLM TP=2 inference on dual R9700 (gfx1201/RDNA4) · Issue #5480 · ROCm/rocm-systems · GitHub

[Issue]: Radeon AI PRO R9700 4card failed in rccl-tests · Issue #162 · ROCm/rccl-tests · GitHub

What’s your use case here? Is it multi-user concurrent inference, or just your own usage?

Some facts to consider:

The gold contacts on PCI-e cards are limited to about 200 cycles. After that the reliability of the card is not guaranteed

When running LLM’s which don’t fit into the memory of a single card, you will need to consider the fact that bandwidth between cards can be a limiting factor in certain scenario’s.

Intel’s software stack for inference is so far behind the curve that you are going to have to put in a lot of effort to make it work for anything that is not specifically made to run on intel hardware. It’s not impossible, but the AMD experience is a lot easier in comparison.

0xDE57:

The mobo has: 3 PCIe 4.0 x16 Slots, 3 PCIe 4.0 x1 Slots, so in theory it could take all 3 cards if I get a bigger case?

First hard lesson everyone gets when setting up their own LLM system is how many PCIe lanes your CPU/MB can actually give.

The Ryzen 5900X has 24 PCIe 4.0 lanes total. 16 go to PCIE1, 4 go to M2_1, and 4 go to the chipset uplink. So those 3 PCIe 4.0 x16 Slots are physically x16-sized connectors, but electrically they’re x16 / x4 / x2.

Additionally, the middle and bottom slots are connected to the chipset, and the X570 chipset connects to the CPU through a single PCIe 4.0 x4 uplink ( giving roughly 8 GB/s in each direction). So PCIE4 and PCIE6 don’t just have fewer lanes individually, they’re sharing that x4 bottleneck with each other, M2_2, SATA, USB, and networking.

You’ll be fine with one card. Two may be usable, the third is gonna be struggling to breath… Not saying you can’t start with that setup, but if you want to get a 2nd card you’ll want to look at a MB that can do true 8x/8x Gen4. GIGABYTE X570 Aorus Pro being one example for an AM4 MB.

 0xDE57:

Coming into this late, but…for what it’s worth, I have a pair of R9700s. I was initially running them with one in the x16 slot, one in a physically-x16-but-electrically-x4 slot hanging off the chipset; the result was a 30-40% performance penalty on that card. This was nothing to do with the bandwidth (there was no communication between the cards, I was using Vulkan with llama.cpp), and everything to do with the extra hop through the chipset. The only practical solution was to get a motherboard with x8/x8 split on the x16 slots.

Also, for what it’s worth, you should really ditch Ollama and move to llama.cpp - it has much better performance and it has router mode now, which gives you everything Ollama does (including the web UI) except for the interactive downloads of models. Even when you take into account the tweakery you’ll inevitably dive into, it’s still less hassle than vLLM (IMO).

posts.text:
Video Soon! Posting this early since many of you have messaged with this set of problems on 2 or 4 R9700s!

How to Run vLLM with Tensor Parallelism Across 4× AMD Radeon R9700 GPUs
todo: There is some really cool multi-token prediction stuff coming (MTP) .. I am still working on that. Lots of smart people here on the forum! If you’ve had success, or failure, with that share your stories and links below.

Last Updated Date: 2026-05-21

Main Test System: AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7980X, 64 GB RAM, 4× AMD Radeon AI PRO R9700 (RDNA4/gfx1201), 31.9 usable GiB VRAM each

ROCm: 6.4.3 kernel driver, ROCk module 6.12.12  (note this is a bit fungible – see context in guide)

 
Table of Contents

The Problem

Root Cause

Two Working Approaches

Quick Start

Step-by-Step Guide

Benchmark Results

Troubleshooting

Docker Command Reference

References

1. The Problem
When starting vLLM with --tensor-parallel-size 2 or --tensor-parallel-size 4 on a system with 2+ AMD Radeon R9700 (gfx1201/RDNA4) GPUs, the server may appear to start (routes register, /v1/models responds), but:

Both GPUs immediately spin at 100% utilization

Inference requests hang indefinitely (no timeout, no response)

Ctrl+C may not kill the process — requires docker kill or kill -9

TP=1 works flawlessly on the same hardware

There are three distinct issues that affect RDNA4 multi-GPU:

Note: I also recommend disabling sleep/wake as this may be related to reports of RDNA4 fans that just… stop working or get locked to 30%. If you are experiencing these types of issues, I want to know and I want to know more about your system!

Issue A: RCCL Tuning Index Bug (affects vLLM ≥0.19)
This might be what led you here if you did a search. It can be quite frustrating to get more than 1 R9700 working, and it’s a series of innocent-ish bugs that, when strung together, cause RDNA for machine learning to fail in frustrating and catastrophic ways.

RCCL librccl.so.1.0.70201 (ROCm 7.2.x) is missing the rcclGetTuningIndexForArch() mapping for gfx1201 → tuning index 7. It falls back to tuning index 0 (designed for MI50/gfx906), selecting an incompatible AllReduce protocol that deadlocks.

Fix tracked in: ROCm/rccl PR #2166

Workaround (Approach A): NCCL_PROTO=Simple env var bypasses the broken LL protocol.

Workaround (Approach B): Use a different ROCm stack (vllm-dev image) that doesn’t have this bug.

Issue B: Shared-Memory Broadcast Hang (affects vLLM ≥0.21.0)
vLLM v0.21.0 (:latest tag) has an additional hang in shm_broadcast.py for larger models (Qwen3.6, gpt-oss-120B) on AMD.

Workaround: Use vLLM v0.20.2 (Approach A) or the vllm-dev image (Approach B).

Issue C: PCIe Topology Assumptions
Per the vLLM GitHub issue #40980 discussion, vLLM’s RCCL integration historically assumes GPUs are behind a PCIe bridge/switch (common in datacenter setups). Consumer RDNA4 cards connected directly to CPU PCIe lanes don’t have this topology, and the default tuning selects algorithms incompatible with direct CPU-attached GPUs. This causes problems on NVIDIA too, but the consequences are more catastrophic on AMD because RCCL’s LL protocol deadlocks rather than gracefully degrading.

There might actually be more bugs than these at work here – I will update as I learn more. This has been a tough one to get my head around.

What Doesn’t Work
These common workarounds from NVIDIA setups do NOT help on RDNA4:

Attempt
Result

--enforce-eager
 No effect

NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1
 No effect (this works for rccl-tests but NOT vLLM)

--disable-custom-all-reduce
 No effect

VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn
 No effect

Using vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:latest (v0.21.0)
 Also deadlocks (ROCm 7.2.2 userspace + shm_broadcast hang)

Using rocm/vllm:latest (v0.10.1)
 Also deadlocks (RCCL 2.22.3 too old)

2. Root Cause
The RCCL Tuning Index Bug
The definitive root cause was identified by srinivamd in vLLM Issue #40980:

RCCL librccl.so.1.0.70201 (shipped with ROCm 7.2.x) is missing the rcclGetTuningIndexForArch() function that maps gfx1201 (RDNA4/Navi4) to tuning index 7. Without this mapping, RCCL silently applies tuning index 0 — designed for MI50/gfx906 PCIe topology — to gfx1201’s PCIe-only dual-GPU configuration. The resulting algorithm/protocol selection is incompatible with RDNA4, causing the AllReduce operation to deadlock indefinitely.

Community Bisect

RCCL Version
ROCm Version
TP=2 Works?

librccl.so.1.0.70101
7.1.1
 Yes

librccl.so.1.0.70201
7.2.x
 Deadlocks

The Permanent Fix
ROCm/rccl PR #2166 adds {"gfx1201", 7} to src/graph/tuning.cc — not yet shipped in any release.

Why Two Approaches?
There are two independent ways to work around the bug:

Approach A (NCCL_PROTO=Simple) forces RCCL to use the Simple protocol instead of the broken LL protocol. This works with the standard vLLM v0.20.2 ROCm image.

Approach B (AITER + vllm-dev) uses a different ROCm stack (v7.0 pre-release) that doesn’t have the tuning index bug at all. It also enables AITER-accelerated MoE kernels, which is required for GPTQ-quantized models.

I think, but I am not sure, the second approach will be more forward-compatible with things like MTP?

3. Two Working Approaches
Approach A: NCCL_PROTO=Simple (vLLM v0.20.2)
Best for: Most models, simple setup, works with any vLLM-compatible model format

Docker image: vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:v0.20.2

Key env var: -e NCCL_PROTO=Simple

ROCm version in image: 7.2.2 (works despite host being 6.4.3)

Confirmed working: All Llama, DeepSeek, Qwen models

Approach B: AITER + vllm-dev Image (vLLM v0.17.0)
Best for: GPTQ-quantized models, no NCCL_PROTO needed, AITER-accelerated MoE

Docker image: rocm/vllm-dev:upstream_preview_releases_v0.17.0_20260303

Key env vars: VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1, HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION=12.0.1

ROCm version in image: 7.0.51831 (pre-release)

Confirmed working: Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-GPTQ-Int4 (39.9 tok/s at TP=4)

mathew2214:

It’s the same issue with the Cycling world. I’ve had conversations with Product Managers on “Why not upgrade this? It would be a $1 part!” $1 turns into $10-$20 by the time you factor in all the costs and extra overhead:

Sourcing the parts

Storing them

Adding the tooling/staff to install that part

The extra step to install the part that may add additional time per unit

Keeping extra on hand for RMA

On top of all that, there are multiple people that touch a product before it makes it to you, and they all want a cut.

Plus, as @starshipeleven correctly pointed out, it would block much needed airflow on top of adding cost.

Basically, there is no upside to adding a video port on a card built to do AI work.

posts.author: starshipeleven
posts.text:
mathew2214:

who the hell needs ten or twenty graphics accelerators? i dont even think a person can watch that many rendered images in a single lifetime.

Computing workloads using GPUs as parallel calculation accelerators (rendering images is basically just highly parallel calculations at the end of the day), and technology like VDI (virtual desktop infrastructure) used to centralize all computers worth of computing power into a couple racks for a large office. It’s an evolution of thin clients, more or less. All workstations in the office are run and images rendered on the server. The people at the desks only have a tiny and weak device that streams the screen like remote desktop. This has advantages for data security, device lifecycle, sometimes helps saving money by purchasing less licenses of expensive workstation software (since now you can easily hot-seat the “workstation” since it’s just a virtual machine), and all sorts of things

 mathew2214:

i thought we were talking gpus, not npus.

AI started in GPUs as a form of professional GPU compute software and still runs on GPUs to this day for the mid end of the spectrum. There are some npus but they are either tiny and extremely weak (meant for basic edge stuff like camera image recognition) or very high end and used only by large businnesses.

Working!!!

Ran a variety of LLMs, and the GPU stays (relatively) cool - in the 70-80C range, so the fan/duct design works. Fan is near-silent, so the GPU-specific fan works well with the 3D-printed duct.

Was somewhat skeptical of my duct design … but it works! 

image1920×1446 796 KB

image1920×1446 681 KB

The low-profile duct fits cleanly into the case.

image1520×2019 526 KB

And temperatures when active are well-controlled.

image1920×1446 587 KB

One more project checked off my list! 

What you need:

AMD Instinct MI25 (duh) - currently under $100 off eBay.

Load the latest WX 9100 BIOS: AMD.WX9100.16384.171219.rom

Needs amdvbflash_linux_4.71 as allows override.

(2x) 6 Pin to 8 Pin PCIe Adapter Power Cable - https://www.microcenter.com/product/615426/6_Pin_to_8_Pin_PCIe_Adapter_Power_Cable_-_Black-_Yellow

GPU fan - BFB1012SHA01 - https://www.ebay.com/sch/i.html?_nkw=BFB1012SHA01&_sacat=0&_from=R40&_trksid=p2332490.m570.l1313

Custom 3D printed duct (no link yet)

Rather a lot of your time. 

To adapt the card you need to:

Remove the stock cover (save the screws).

Attach the GPU fan (needs 2mm screws) though the existing holes in the card.

Plug in the fan’s 4-pin connector to the card.

Glue down the fan-cable to keep away from the fan.

Attach the custom duct using same holes/screws as for original cover.

That gets you working GPU hardware.

Also, IMHO this is a much cleaner solution than the existing offerings. 

You also want ROCm 5.7, as the last version to support the MI25 / WX9100. Easiest to just run this in a pre-built Docker image. If you want a native install, this pretty much locks you to Ubuntu 22 (not 24), as the latest version compatible with ROCm 5.7.

Well, went down the rabbit-hole.

Was not satisfied with my prior install of Ubuntu 22 / ROCm / ollama on the server. Started over.

Again, the AI (Microsoft Copilot) was hugely helpful, saved me a lot of time, but also needed help.

Seems ROCm 5.7 does not want to use the WX9100. Also seems for fan support we really want the AMD ATOMBIOS PowerPlay tables from the WX9100 copied into the MI25 BIOS.

There are somewhat-disused existing tools … that do not work.

Well, let us see just how much these AI-tools can do. Opened up vscode with example BIOS files from the MI25 and WX9100 cards, and started iterating on code to parse ATOMBIOS data and copy in/out PowerPlay tables.

The first iteration was wrong - failed to dump known/good BIOS files.

When prompted, Copilot iterated until the dump worked.

Asked for options to save/load the PowerPlay tables. Tried and failed to load an MI25 BIOS with WX9100 tables. Then …

image1145×144 11.3 KB

Ironic since the aim of this exercise is to use a local LLM … 

Tool is at:

https://github.com/pbannister/amd_atombios

LATER: Note that I abandoned this approach as the MI25 BIOS, even with fan parameters in the “PP” tables (set at runtime), seems to be incapable of proper fan control. (see next)

posts.author: Preston_Bannister
posts.text:
So … this was tedious. Seems use of the MI25 BIOS is best supported for running LLMs. But the MI25 BIOS lacks (working) fan control. Copying the fan control parameters from the WX9100 into the MI25 BIOS is possible, but flashing the modified BIOS fails.

Turns out we can modify the BIOS fan control parameters at runtime (through the “pp_table” sysfs file) … but in the end the MI25 BIOS just does not seem to do fan control properly. (So even if we could flash a modified BIOS, it would still not work.)

Where this ends is created a service that runs a script to actively monitor and control the MI25 fan. So far, this seems to work. The needed scripts are in:

  

      github.com

infr — a pure-Rust, Vulkan-first LLM inference engine (testers wanted!)

Hey all,

I’ve been building infr, a pure-Rust LLM inference engine written from the metal up — no llama.cpp/ggml underneath. The only non-Rust parts are the GPU driver calls and the compute shaders.

The idea: one inference server that runs on any mainstream GPU via Vulkan (AMD / NVIDIA / Intel), with a native Metal backend for Apple Silicon, plus a CPU reference backend. It pulls GGUF models straight from HuggingFace, has a terminal chat, and an OpenAI-compatible server. Currently runs Llama, Qwen2/3/3.5/3.6 (dense + MoE), Gemma 3/4 (including E2B), and DiffusionGemma — and it benchmarks competitively with llama.cpp on my RX 7900 XTX (there’s a built-in infr compare that runs both side by side).

Repo: GitHub - kryptic-sh/infr: Pure-Rust, Vulkan-first LLM inference engine · GitHub

Where I need help: it’s only been seriously tested on my own hardware. If you have a Vulkan-capable GPU (especially NVIDIA or Intel Arc — AMD is well covered) or a Mac to exercise the Metal backend, I’d love to hear what works, what breaks, and what the infr bench / infr compare numbers look like on your card. Issues and terminal dumps welcome, no Rust knowledge needed — infr pull + infr run and you’re chatting.

Thanks for reading — and in the spirit of full disclosure: this post was written by the same kind of thing the project runs.

posts.author: digitalscream
posts.text:
OK, as always, a few questions…

What models are you trying to run?

What do you want to do with those models? Agentic stuff/code/just chat/all of the above/etc?

How many parallel requests do you plan on actually using (ie not just for benchmarks)?

What’s your reasoning in trying to get vLLM running?

Have you tried llama.cpp?

Tensor parallelism isn’t the be-all-and-end-all. In fact, there are a number of cases where it’s not even the best option.

EDIT: OK, I’ve got a few minutes here, so why not…

vLLM is not the best option for anything except when you’re handling 8-16+ concurrent requests. It’s also the most painful to set up, so…

…llama.cpp is your best bet. Download the binaries for Ubuntu from the GitHub releases.

If you’re running dense models (eg Qwen 3.6 27B), then ROCm + tensor split will be faster by about 25%.

If you’re running MoE models (eg Qwen 3.6 35B), then Vulkan + layer split will be faster by about 50%. Don’t forget to set RADV_DEBUG=nocompute when launching the server.

If you’re not running parallel requests at all, then use MTP for a significant boost in TG, although you’ll pay a penalty in PP.

If you have the power budget available, use LACT to overclock the VRAM to ~2750MHz, and up the power limit to 330W.

To give you an idea, on my dual R9700 system…

Qwen 3.6 27B

llama.cpp + ROCm + tensor split = 1800t/s PP, 40t/s TG

llama.cpp + ROCm + tensor split + MTP = 1200t/s PP, 75-80t/s TG

llama.cpp + Vulkan + layer split = 1600t/s PP, 30t/s TG

llama.cpp + Vulkan + layer split + MTP = 1100t/s PP, 45-55t/s TG

Qwen 3.6 35B A3B

llama.cpp + ROCm + tensor split = 3100t/s PP, 70t/s TG

llama.cpp + ROCm + layer split = 3700t/s PP, 70t/s TG

llama.cpp + Vulkan + layer split = 5400t/s PP, 120t/s TG

llama.cpp + Vulkan + layer split + MTP = 2900t/s PP, 140-180t/s TG

Note that this is using the Lemonade ROCm distribution of llama.cpp - I haven’t got ROCm installed on the system, because it seems to override the amdgpu driver and causes performance problems with Vulkan (and my main models are all MoE, so Vulkan is my priority).

posts.author: digitalscream
posts.text:
Strawberry:

I’d like to run Qwen3.6 or future models in that size range.

Size isn’t everything, active parameters are. Dense models like Qwen 3.6 27B activate all the parameters for every token, whereas Mixture of Experts models like Qwen 3.6 35B A3B only activate the “A3B” part - so 3B parameters. That’s why they run faster with a higher total parameter count.

 Strawberry:

My reasoning is (and I might be wrong) that using tensor parallelism, you can fully utilize the hardware because you don’t need the cards to constantly back and forth, you front load the memory division.

The logic is based on a faulty assumption - that all models and architectures behave the same way, and therefore tensor parallelism will always be faster. The fact is that llama.cpp layer split with Vulkan is faster than any implementation that uses ROCm…for MoE models and smaller dense models, basically up to around 20B active parameters. Past that point, ROCm with tensor parallelism tends to take over.

I honestly wouldn’t bother with ROCm - for your uses, most of the time, Vulkan will likely be faster if you’re using the 35B MoE model. If you want to experiment with ROCm, then remove it from your system (and reinstall Mesa), and then use the Lemonade llamacpp-rocm portable distribution instead. Much easier to manage.

 Strawberry:

I have not tried llama.cpp outside of LM-Studio because from my understanding it’s the same thing under the hood, just without an easy gui to configure it. (I may also be wrong here)

Again, I’m afraid that’s a faulty (albeit totally understandable) assumption. The GUI abstracts away a lot of the tuneable parameters of llama.cpp, to the point where it’s almost always ~40% slower than llama.cpp running raw. It’s always a fair bit behind the latest nightly builds of llama.cpp, and they release 3-4 times per day. A lot of optimisations go in every week.

 Strawberry:

According to your statement here, I’m probably doing just fine. Maybe a bit mysteriously slow, but without an overclock, and limited to PCIe gen4, maybe that explains it?

Not really - I’m running my R9700s on PCIE 4.0 x8 each. The overclocks help by around 10%, but that’s it.

My advice - download the latest Ubuntu/Vulkan release of llama.cpp from their GitHub repo. Run llama-server in router mode (ie don’t point it at a model, point it at a directory containing your GGUFs), and see what that gives you - router mode comes with a web UI built in. I run it as a systemd service:

[Unit]
Description=Start llama.cpp service
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=lj
Environment="RADV_DEBUG=nocompute"
WorkingDirectory=/path/to/llama.cpp/directory
ExecStart=/path/to/llama.cpp/directory/llama-server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 --models-dir /path/to/models/directory --models-preset /path/to/models/directory/config.ini --models-max 1 --cache-ram 16384
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

The RADV_DEBUG=nocompute is really important if you’re on Mesa 26.0 or above and you’re not using either of the GPUs for actual graphics - the graphics queue on the R9700 is faster than the compute queue. That’s usually worth a good 5-10% boost in TG, but if you’re using either GPU for a GUI then you’ll find it stutters like hell if you use this option.

The config.ini is where you configure all the model-specific optimisations (you can select the loaded model from within the web UI). It basically consists of repeated sections that look like this, which is basically just the command line arguments for llama-server organised by model:

[agent_35B]
mmap=0
ctx-size=262144
flash-attn=on
batch-size=2048
ubatch-size=1024
model=/path/to/models/directory/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q6_K_XL.gguf
n-predict=-1
n-gpu-layers=999
threads=1
top-p       = 0.95
top-k       = 20
temp        = 0.6
repeat-penalty = 1.0
split-mode = layer
reasoning = off
spec-type = draft-mtp
spec-draft-n-max = 3

(you probably don’t want to use MTP, since you want parallel execution, so get rid of the last two lines)

Finally…don’t forget that LACT can be managed remotely. Very handy…but can also result in doing silly things and not being able to immediately recover. I tripped the protection in my 850W power supply a few times before I realised that running in tensor split mode pushed both GPUs to the limit…and the actual usage is usually 70W+ past what nvtop is telling you (upwards of 400W each when the limit’s set at 330W). Given that you’re running a Threadripper 3000 series and a pair of R9700s, you absolutely don’t want to do that unless you’ve got a 1200W+ PSU.

Incidentally, I found that one of my GPUs could do 2800MHz VRAM, but the other can only manage 2750MHz. I erred on the side of caution and went with the lower value, as well as a 50mV undervolt.

Hope that’s enough to get you started

One thing you should know about the Lemonade build is that it doesn’t include RCCL (AMD’s version of NCCL for P2P), which should - in theory - allow P2P communication when running in tensor split mode. posts.author: Waylon_R
posts.text:
Claude says (we fought this fight together):

You’re not missing something obvious, and it’s not a marketing lie. You walked into a real, specific, still-unfixed bug — and then a second one on top of it. I run the same two cards (dual R9700, Z690), so this is all first-hand.

Problem 1: you’re on Ubuntu 26.04.

ROCm 7.2.x supports 24.04 LTS. It does not support 26.04. If you’ve been on 26.04 this whole time, you likely never had a working ROCm userspace at all — which means vLLM was structurally impossible no matter what else you did. LM-Studio “working” is consistent with this: it’s running llama.cpp on the Vulkan/Mesa backend, which doesn’t touch ROCm. That’s why it’s the only thing that works.

Go to Ubuntu 24.04.4, install ROCm 7.2.x via amdgpu-install, and confirm rocminfo lists two gfx1201 agents before you try anything else. Do not set HSA_OVERRIDE_GFX_VERSION — the R9700 is natively supported and overriding it breaks things.

Kernel cmdline (Threadripper): amd_iommu=on iommu=pt pcie_aspm=off amdgpu.runpm=0. The last one keeps the second card from dropping into a low-power state where it stops enumerating properly.

Problem 2: the RCCL tuning-index deadlock. This is the one that ate your week.

RCCL in ROCm 7.2.x (librccl.so.1.0.70201) is missing the tuning-table mapping for gfx1201. It silently falls back to tuning index 0 — which is the table for MI50/gfx906 — and that selects an LL-protocol AllReduce that deadlocks forever on RDNA4. Both GPUs pin at 100% and nothing ever comes back. Community bisect confirms it: librccl.so.1.0.70101 (ROCm 7.1.1) works, 70201 (7.2.x) hangs.

The fix is one environment variable:

-e NCCL_PROTO=Simple

That’s it. That’s the week.

Important details people get wrong:

NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 works for rccl-tests but not for vLLM. Different bug.

--enforce-eager, --disable-custom-all-reduce, and VLLM_WORKER_MULTIPROC_METHOD=spawn do not help the deadlock.

Alternative if you’d rather not carry an env var: run a pre-7.2 image such as rocm/vllm-dev:upstream_preview_releases_v0.17.0_20260303 (RCCL 2.26.6), which doesn’t have the regression.

Status as of today: the permanent fix is RCCL PR #2166 (“Navi4 default tuning enablement”). It was opened March 4, approved by a maintainer March 12, and is still open and unmerged. Production ROCm is 7.2.4 and still ships RCCL 2.27.7. So assume every 7.2.x release has this bug until you see it in a changelog.

The guide you need is already on this forum: Wendell’s AMD Radeon R9700 Linux TP2 and TP4 — the Definitive Guide (/t/amd-radeon-r9700-linux-tp2-and-tp4-the-definitive-guide/250504). TP=2 and TP=4 working switch-free on plain root-complex topology, ~65 tok/s on Llama-3.1-8B at TP=2. Also worth reading: Dual R9700’s AMD VLLM-Container woes (/t/dual-r9700s-amd-vllm-container-woes/250053).

Two things that aren’t bugs, so you stop chasing them:

“70 tok/s, GPU utilization 33%.” That’s normal. Single-stream autoregressive decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound. 30–40% utilization is what a healthy card looks like doing that work. It is not a symptom of anything.

Tensor parallelism is not the speedup you think it is. TP=2 on an 8B gets you ~65 tok/s vs ~61 at TP=4 — the cross-card traffic eats most of the win on a root-complex topology. TP’s real value is fitting a model that doesn’t fit on one card. If your actual goal is “serve an OpenAI-compatible endpoint at full context for cline/cursor/etc,” strongly consider llama.cpp + llama-swap with one model per card instead. Less exotic, doesn’t touch RCCL at all, and for a single-user endpoint it will likely feel the same or better.

One warning before you get TP working: tensor-split is the only mode that drives both cards to full power simultaneously. R9700 is rated 300W TBP but transients spike toward ~400W. People on this forum have tripped OCP on an 850W PSU doing exactly this, right at the moment TP finally started working — and then blamed the software. If you get a hard reboot the first time TP succeeds, look at the PSU, not RCCL. LACT can cap power if you need a stopgap.

Good luck. The frustration is warranted; the conclusion isn’t.

posts.author: Waylon_R
posts.text:
Worth putting the reasoning on the record, because I think it reframes the OP’s whole problem.

When I built my stack (dual R9700, RAG pipeline, OpenAI-compatible endpoint — basically the OP’s stated goal) I went Vulkan-only for decode and deliberately did not use ROCm for serving. Four reasons, in descending order of how load-bearing they turned out to be:

1. Vulkan is just faster on RDNA4. ~183 tok/s Vulkan vs ~150 tok/s ROCm HIP on Qwen3-30B-A3B Q4_K_M (llama.cpp GitHub Discussion #19890), corroborated by Phoronix’s “AMD ROCm 7.1 vs. RADV Vulkan For Llama.cpp With The Radeon AI PRO R9700.” I’ve been carrying 35–45% on decode as the working figure. @digitalscream’s +40% lands right on top of that, from an independent stack.

2. Flash Attention works on the Vulkan path. The Vulkan FA shader path is independent of the ROCm CK kernels that HIP uses, so -fa is available and validated on gfx1201. Non-trivial: it cut my 16K compute buffer by ~86%, +17% decode, +27% prefill. That’s the difference between fitting a model at full context and not.

3. FP8 is broken on gfx1201 in the 7.2.x stack. vLLM mis-detects it and silently dequantizes to FP32 (vllm #28649); AITER/TransformerEngine silently falls back rather than erroring (ROCm #520). Note silently — you don’t get told, you just get a slow model and no explanation. If you’re chasing vLLM specifically to get FP8 throughput on these cards right now, you’re chasing something that isn’t there.

4. No collectives = no RCCL = no bug. Every model I run fits on one 32GB card, so nothing ever crosses cards. Which means the tuning-index deadlock that ate the OP’s week isn’t something I work around — it’s out of scope by construction. That’s an architectural choice with real leverage: you can design the entire class of problem out of existence rather than env-var your way past it.

Clarification: OH ALSO I should have been more clear about this:

USB4 is 4 lanes-- each lane is up to 20 gigabit BUT unlike what we call PCIe lanes, each lane here is simplex. It is TX or RX. USB4 is 2 TX and 2 RX, each lane is UP TO 20 gigabit.

On Thunderbolt 5 that’s how you can do 120x40 or 80x80. It’s still 4 lanes, but the speed is bumped to 40 gigabit PER LANE. So you can still do 2 + 2 for 80 tx and 80 rx OR 3 + 1 for 120 tx and 40 rx. That’s why it’s asymmetric. I said that in the video too but I get how it might not have been clear.

Our Strix Halo cluster is capped at 20 gigabit each way, 40 gigabit but its not 40 gigabits each way, its 20 gigabits each way.

I was hoping new kernel/drivers would let us have 2x20 gigabit lanes worth of bandwidth between the hosts, 40 gigabit each way, but that doesn’t seem to be the case.

Ran your suite on an independent pair, since a second data point on different chassis seemed useful. Same APU both ends, deliberately mismatched form factors:

node0 — GMKtec EVO-X3 (Ryzen AI MAX+ 395), kernel 7.0.0-29-generic

node1 — ASUS ProArt PX13 HN7306EAC (same APU, laptop), same kernel

Direct USB4 cable, thunderbolt0 on 10.55.0.0/30, MTU 65520

rx_speed=20.0 Gb/s tx_speed=20.0 Gb/s, rx_lanes=2 tx_lanes=2, generation=4

Measured with a document-parsing service resident on both nodes (load ~1.0), so these are loaded-machine numbers, not a quiesced lab

What this adds
Your ~8.85 Gbit/s reproduces almost exactly on completely different hardware — 8.88 one way, 9.41 the other. Given your lane clarification upthread (2 TX + 2 RX, capped 20 Gb/s each way), we’re sitting at the same ~50 % of per-direction line rate you are.

The two directions don’t contend. Running --bidir gets 10.1 and 10.2 Gbit/s at the same time, so each direction independently hits its own ~50 % ceiling rather than sharing one. That’s consistent with the CPU-side encapsulation/copy theory rather than anything shared in the fabric — and it means the zero-copy work in 7.2 you mentioned has roughly 2× headroom per direction to claw back, not 2× total.

Parallel streams buy nothing — 8.88 → 8.90, 9.41 → 9.43. One TCP stream already saturates the path.

A ~6 % direction asymmetry shows up on Thunderbolt too, stable across repeats (laptop→mini-PC faster). You’d noted asymmetry on Ethernet but described TB as symmetric.

On the second link not coming up
You mentioned you couldn’t get the other link up and would try another Strix Halo. Data point: our two boxes differ. The ProArt PX13 laptop enumerates two USB4 domains (domain0, domain1); the EVO-X3 mini-PC enumerates only domain0. So on a mixed pair you’re capped by whichever chassis exposes one domain, and it looks like a driver problem when it’s really the box. Cheap to check on both ends before digging:

ls /sys/bus/thunderbolt/devices/domain*

On the 858 µs RDMA latency spikes
You put those down to scheduler interference. First thing we’d rule out is platform power management, especially on a laptop chassis. We pin the ProArt to performance platform_profile + governor + EPP via a systemd unit at boot, because the stock balanced/powersave defaults cost us roughly 2× on real GPU throughput — a bigger effect than anything interconnect-side we’ve touched. Our TB minimum is 35 µs against your 119 µs, and our max 0.714 ms against your 1.119 ms, on a loaded box.

@wer’s question — what actually runs across this today
Since you asked what the entry point is and what speaks RDMA, here’s our operational experience rather than a benchmark:

vLLM tensor-parallel (TP=2) across the link via Ray works on this hardware over plain TCP/IP over thunderbolt0 — no RDMA, no custom driver. That’s the workload where your 66 µs vs ~500 µs latency gap should actually pay, because per-layer all-reduce is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound. We have not produced a clean TP=1 vs TP=2 comparison, so we’re not going to quote a speedup — but that’s the experiment that would justify the soft-RoCE work far better than ib_send_bw will.

Embarrassingly parallel work doesn’t need any of this. Our document-parsing service fans whole files out to both nodes and scales 2.14× on two nodes. Payloads are whole documents, so the interconnect is nowhere near the critical path. If your workload looks like this, TCP over TB is already overkill and RDMA buys you nothing.

The honest summary is that the interconnect has not yet been our bottleneck — power/thermal policy and memory sizing have both cost us more.

One Strix-Halo-specific trap for anyone clustering these
GTT is carved from the same 128 GB the OS runs in — “GPU memory” and “system memory” are one pool. Setting --gpu-memory-utilization the way you would on a discrete card starves the host: we put a node into a ~25-minute swap storm that needed a power cycle. We now reserve 24 GiB for the host and cap at 0.72. Related: a resident vision model’s activation high-water grew GTT from 12 GB to 67 GB under real documents — allocator peak, never returned — which on a unified-memory box is indistinguishable from a leak in free. Both bite as soon as you start pinning real workloads to two of these.

Happy to run the soft-RoCE/RXE half of your suite on 7.0.0-29 if a second kernel data point is useful before 7.2 lands.

posts.author: Ray519
posts.text:
wendell:

USB4 is 4 lanes-- each lane is up to 20 gigabit BUT unlike what we call PCIe lanes, each lane here is simplex. It is TX or RX

USB itself defines it much like PCIe, where a Lane is always bidirectional and USB4 only has 2 lanes. With USB4 Gen 4 they just leave the lane concept behind. In USB language, your are talking about wire-pairs here.

 wendell:

I was hoping new kernel/drivers would let us have 2x20 gigabit lanes worth of bandwidth between the hosts, 40 gigabit each way, but that doesn’t seem to be the case.

This single-lane on cross-domain connections seems to be a chipset side limitation. I have no idea why this is allowed for USB4 Gen 2 and Gen 3 speeds, as I cannot come up with a good reason why a dual lane controller would be allowed to only support single lane operation in cross-domain mode (which on the physical level should be the same as non-cross-domain). But it seems to have been grandfathered in due to the structure of USB4 and TB1-3 before it (establish each lane separately and THEN go through a bonding phase). And not supporting bonding on cross domain connections is explicitly allowed for in the USB4 spec (I saw it once while browsing through the spec).

I have also found no way in that controllers report that they have this limit. Its just the connection manager (driver) requesting dual lane operation and the chipset ignoring it on cross-domain links, like it would if bonding fails for other reasons like a half-broken cable etc.

(The chipset reports single lane / dual lane operation on each lane. So if bonding succeeded, the bits flip to dual-lane mode, with the final choice being down to the chipset and its firmware and the entire system including opposing controller and cable needing to support it successfully).

We have seen some reports of Intel chipsets doing dual-lane cross-domain (like a Tiger Lake cluster on Linux), so there absolutely are 40G controllers out there that do support it. But since its unclear to me if we can use Windows just to diagnose whether a controller can do it (and you need to be very sure the opposing side is also capable of dual-lane cross-domain) we have no set list of controllers that will do it and those that won’t.

Since the Linux USB4 driver seems to do it on the right Intel chipsets, most likely the current AMD USB4 controllers just cannot do it (at least on current firmware).

Because USB4 Gen 4 no longer thinks in lanes and does not have a bonding phase like Gen 2 and Gen 3 has, this is no longer a thing on Gen 4 links. There you should always get 80G/80G, only limited by the mailbox and potentially the PCIe bandwidth to that mailbox on external controllers.

Edit: oh, there is one mention in the current USB4 Connection Manager Guidelines

posts.author: wendell
posts.text:
Your company is probably spending too much on AI: Switchyard, local models, routing, and the data flywheel

  
    
  

So I have been working on an enterprise consulting project where the plan is “adopt AI” but my go-to IT toolbox is monitoring and management of “how” and “what” the users are doing (before “AI” even enters the picture).

The changes/improvements to SwitchYard and the release of Nemoton Lightning are two missing puzzle pieces that, imho, will solve the last missing bits for managing “responsible” and non-IT AI use cases in an organization. Or, at least, give you ammo and documentation to push back against misunderstanding how to apply the tools at the c-suite level.

Look… this isn’t complicated. I want away from the AI hype tulip bulb mania. Management has wildly wildly different ideas about how AI might be used in an organization than the reality of how it will actually be used. I want to capture the reality data to push back on the hype/hallucinations/ai psychosis/whatever you want to call it.

Finally, we have effective tools to take action in a meaningful way with only a tiny fraction of the effort a year ago.

That data is a shield to protect my sanity for two reasons.. re-alignment with reality and to have the foundations of a process where we actually get measurable artifacts to know the efficacy of the tools we’re deployng.

The short version:

Commodity intelligence → routing → observable execution → evaluation → data exhaust → specialization → cheaper local intelligence → fewer frontier calls → repeat.

                    
            
          

                    
            
          

We did a video a while back on using HAProxy for HA but… expand that to “model router” and then telemetry on what users are trying to do.

I think this is where enterprise AI is heading, and NVIDIA’s Switchyard update plus Nemotron 3.5 Lightning makes the whole thing much more accessible.

It’s not another model release – it’s the last piece of software you need for this whole ecosystem that’s required to stop sending every stupid little task to a frontier model.

It is finally becoming paint-by-numbers enough for normal IT people to deploy, measure, customize and improve.

That is going to have two consequences:

Economic: frontier inference becomes an exception rather than the default.

Organizational: the company stops renting all of its intelligence and starts accumulating some of its own.

What’s Running In The Video
My demonstrator is an HP Z8 Fury with two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs.

20260811_1207031920×1440 558 KB

On it I have:

Switchyard as the model router.

A small local model.

A much larger local model, currently DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731.

RAG/vector infrastructure.

Evaluation and logging.

(The frontier API is still available. It just isn’t the first thing every request gets thrown at.)

Switchyard sits between the application and all of those resources. The current public implementation can translate OpenAI Chat, OpenAI Responses and Anthropic Messages formats, then route requests to things like vLLM, NIM, Ollama and OpenAI-compatible endpoints. It supports classifier routing, stage routing, escalation and custom routing policies. Claude Code and Codex can both be launched through it. (Switchyard Magic!)

So the application does not need to particularly care whether the answer came from a 3B-active local model, a big local model, a server elsewhere in the building, or Opus.

That is the point.

This idea did not appear suddenly on a crisp Tuesday afternoon
This wasn’t really in any of NVIDIA’s press release stuff, but in my mind (and I could be a crazy person) there is a pretty obvious research trail here:

In 2023, FrugalGPT showed that cascades of models could match the best individual model with dramatically lower cost, or improve accuracy at a fixed cost. (FrugalGPT)

In 2024, RouteLLM formalized learning when to send a request to a strong or weak model. (RouteLLM)

NVIDIA followed with its own cost-efficient LLM Router Blueprint. (NVIDIA LLM Router Blueprint)

Then NVIDIA Research published a paper with the wonderfully unsubtle title Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI . Their recommendation is almost exactly what I am arguing here: use small models for repetitive narrow agent work, specialize them, and build heterogeneous systems that reserve large general-purpose models for the difficult stuff. (paper)

Then came ToolOrchestra and Nemotron-Orchestrator-8B .

An 8B orchestrator was trained to decide when to use other models and tools. In NVIDIA’s evaluation, the resulting system scored 37.1% on Humanity’s Last Exam versus 35.1% for GPT-5, at about 30% of the monetary cost and 2.5x the speed. (ToolOrchestra paper, NVIDIA project page)

That’s not  “an 8B model is smarter than GPT-5”  but the system was better at the task.

The orchestrator could assemble the resources actually required instead of asking one enormous model to cosplay as omniscience.

(This is also a bit of the philosophy in our own Turnstone project with MCP, Skills, tool calling, etc)

Nemotron 3.5 Lightning
NVIDIA’s prerelease material for Tuesday describes Nemotron 3.5 Lightning as a 30B MoE with 3B active parameters , aimed at high-volume agent execution and low latency. Long-running agentic tasks.

It includes multi-token prediction and speculative decoding support, plus DFlash and DSpark inference optimization. NVIDIA says post-training uses Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation, or MOPD, and that the model was deliberately trained across multiple open-source agent harnesses.

Sure okay, long-running agent tasks BUT it’s got another aspect that everyone’s missing earnestly trying to “do right by their organizations” with AI – customization with low effort and good documentation around that.

NVIDIA says Lightning will be customizable with LoRA or full SFT using NeMo AutoModel and Megatron Bridge, plus reinforcement learning through NeMo RL and NeMo Gym. Weights,

posts.author: martona
posts.text:
Two RTX PRO 6000 Blackwells run $15k apiece, the 128GB of RAM is another $5k, so you’re at $35k before the CPU and storage. At your own cited cost basis of $12-25/M frontier tokens, that money buys roughly 3.5 billion tokens of Opus-class inference  with zero ops burden, zero depreciation. Your $0.015/M marginal figure only works if the box stays busy; you said yourself it’s not TCO, but the whole pitch depends on near-full duty cycle on an asset that’s obsolete in three years.

And the marginal cost comparison ignores the biggest line item: labor. The flywheel you’re describing is an ongoing engineering function. “Paint-by-numbers for normal IT people” is doing a lot of work in this post. One FTE-equivalent of janitor time spent tending the flywheel costs more per year than the frontier bill it displaces.

Meanwhile the price of capability keeps collapsing. Frontier list prices are sticky, but last year’s frontier performance keeps shipping in this year’s cheap tier, hosted, at commodity prices. Whatever your local stack matches today, an API will match at a few dollars per million tokens before the workstation finishes depreciating. You’re racing a falling price curve with $45k of fixed capex.

LLMRouterBench: fancy routers barely beat simple baselines, and there’s a big gap to oracle. If routing is mediocre, you’re either eating quality loss on misrouted-down requests or escalating enough that the frontier bill doesn’t actually shrink.

The telemetry/accountability/dataset argument is good and I wish it were the whole post. But “capture how people actually use AI” doesn’t require two Blackwells; HAProxy logs in front of API calls gets you the same. The observability case and the “more-you-buy-the-more-you-save” case are separable, and you’re not serving your readers’ interests by bundling them.

Big Data is Dead

  Big data is dead. Long live easy data. | Reading time: 18 min read

  
    Reading time: 18 min read
  

  

  
    
    
  

  

An alternate definition of Big Data is “when the cost of keeping data around is less than the cost of figuring out what to throw away.” I like this definition because it encapsulates why people end up with Big Data. It isn’t because they need it; they just haven’t bothered to delete it. If you think about many data lakes that organizations collect, they fit this bill entirely: giant, messy swamps where no one really knows what they hold or whether it is safe to clean them up.

The cost of keeping data around is higher than just the cost to store the physical bytes. Under regulations like GDPR and CCPA, you are required to track all usage of certain types of data. Some data needs to be deleted within a certain period of time. If you have phone numbers in a parquet file that sit around for too long in your data lake somewhere, you may be violating statutory requirements.

wendell:

Management has wildly wildly different ideas about how AI might be used in an organization than the reality of how it will actually be used.

This is the crux of the problem, along with “the reality of what it can actually do reliably”. In my experience, management are astonishingly resistant to any education on the subject. In fact, it’s the main reason I quit my job a few weeks ago.

I interviewed for positions with 11 companies, all of whom displayed exactly the same behaviour - as far as they’re concerned, “AI” = “Fewer developers or the same developers doing 10 times as much work, and by the way we want a chatbot on the website”.

It’s all about quantity, with no discussion of quality or capability allowed. Not just code - that mindset is infecting every business process.

The problem is that, as far as C-suite execs are concerned, generative AI is doing exactly what they want, because the numbers don’t yet reflect the growing snowball of customer dissatisfaction now that it’s not just affecting system stability but business stability. Ticket throughput is up, customer onboarding is up, attrition isn’t the worst it’s ever been, development velocity is up…hell, rank-and-file employee satisfaction is up because they’ve outsourced all their thinking to Claude and they’re not really doing much work at all now.

If there’s one thing we can say with certainty about the adoption of LLMs, it’s that it’s massively highlighted the disconnect between management and reality at the coal face, but the resistance to that concept makes it impossible to prove to people who don’t understand (yet).

Until that disconnect is resolved - which will only really happen with concrete examples of businesses failing - no amount of tech wizardry will help. It’s a human problem, and human nature changes slowly once it’s got hold of an idea that looks like it’s all upsides.

Still, cool idea
